common_name: Baron Solemacher Alpine Strawberry (Runnerless German Heirloom)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, pressing the dust-fine seed onto the soil surface without covering since light aids germination.

directions: Baron Solemacher is a nineteenth-century German heirloom alpine strawberry prized for forming tidy, runnerless clumps rather than spreading by stolons, which makes it well suited to edging, containers, and small raised beds. Surface-sow the tiny seeds indoors and keep them consistently moist at 60-75F, since germination can be slow and uneven over several weeks. Transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light shade after the danger of frost has passed, and expect a light crop the first year with fuller production from year two onward. Plants bear small, intensely aromatic red berries from early summer into fall and are best increased by division every few years once established.

common_name: Yellow Wonder Alpine Strawberry (Pale-Fruited Bird-Resistant Woodland Strawberry)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; the fine seed needs light and steady moisture to germinate.

directions: Yellow Wonder is a day-neutral alpine strawberry that ripens to a pale lemon-gold rather than red, a trait many gardeners value because birds are less likely to spot and peck the fruit before it can be picked. Plants form compact, runnerless clumps and flower and fruit continuously from summer into fall once established. Surface-sow seed indoors, keep evenly moist, and transplant seedlings into rich, well-drained soil in a spot with morning sun and afternoon shade in hot climates. The soft, sweet, low-acid berries have a pineapple-tinged wild-strawberry flavor and bruise easily, so pick and use them promptly rather than storing.

common_name: Mignonette Alpine Strawberry (French Everbearing Woodland Strawberry)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; surface-sow and do not cover, as the tiny seeds need light to germinate.

directions: Mignonette is a compact French heirloom alpine strawberry, considered an improved selection of the old Reine des Vallees type, grown for its dainty pointed red berries and rich woodland-strawberry perfume rather than for size or yield. Plants form neat, semi-evergreen mounds without runners and often produce a light crop the first season from an early indoor sowing. Grow in fertile, moist but well-drained soil; it tolerates partial shade but sets more fruit with several hours of direct sun. Because the berries are small, soft, and quick to perfume a whole bowl, they are best used fresh for snacking, garnishing desserts, or infusing drinks rather than for preserving.

common_name: Improved Rugen Alpine Strawberry (Everbearing German Woodland Strawberry)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; press the fine seed onto a moist starting mix and keep uncovered.

directions: Improved Rugen is a German alpine strawberry selection named for the Baltic island of Ruegen, valued for producing larger-than-typical fruit on plants that send out only a few short runners, so it stays tidier than wild seedling strawberries while still filling in a bed over time. Sow indoors in late winter, surface-sowing the dust-like seed and keeping it consistently moist under bright light. Transplant into rich, well-drained soil after frost danger passes, siting plants where they get a half day of sun; established clumps flower and fruit continuously from late spring into fall. Harvest the aromatic red berries as they ripen, since they soften quickly and do not hold well once picked.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring around the last frost date; Profusion is sterile and produces no viable seed, so it must be propagated by root division.

directions: Profusion is a naturally occurring sterile selection of garden sorrel that never bolts to flower or set seed, so all of the plant's energy stays in leaf production and it can only be increased by dividing an established clump. Plant divisions in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in early spring, spacing them roughly a foot apart in a permanent bed since the plants are long-lived perennials. Because it never diverts energy into flowering, Profusion keeps producing tender, fleshy, mildly tart leaves later into summer heat than seed-grown sorrel, which typically turns tough and bitter once it sets flower stalks. Harvest outer leaves continually through the growing season and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped nursery stock in fall or early spring; alpine currant tolerates deep shade and poor soil better than almost any other fruiting shrub.

directions: Alpine currant is an extremely tough, compact, mound-forming shrub long used for shade hedging in cold climates where few other woody plants tolerate dense shade and dry soil so well. Plant in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil; it is not particular about soil pH or fertility and shrugs off urban pollution and road salt. Inconspicuous greenish-yellow flowers appear in spring, and female plants (this species is dioecious, so both sexes are needed for fruit) set small, glossy red currants in midsummer that are edible but tart and bland, used mainly by birds or for jelly rather than fresh eating. Prune after flowering to maintain a formal hedge shape, since it tolerates shearing extremely well and rarely needs spraying for pests.

planting.note: Plant container-grown nursery stock or rooted cuttings in fall or spring into acidic, gritty, well-drained soil; this circumpolar alpine and arctic native resents heavy, poorly drained ground.

directions: Alpine bearberry is a low, mat-forming, deciduous dwarf shrub of arctic and alpine tundra across the Northern Hemisphere, with small, deeply veined leaves that turn brilliant red in autumn before dropping. It spreads slowly by trailing woody stems that root as they touch the ground, forming a dense evergreen-textured carpet well suited to rock gardens and cold-climate shaded groundcover plantings. Small urn-shaped white to pink flowers in late spring are followed by juicy black berries that ripen through red before turning glossy black; the fruit is edible raw but rather bitter and improves with cooking, and has traditionally been eaten by northern peoples with fat or fish. Site it in acidic, well-drained soil with some shade from hot afternoon sun, since it is adapted to short, cool growing seasons and struggles in warm, humid climates.
